name: Upton Sinclair
role: American novelist, socialist and 1934 Democratic candidate for governor of California (1878-1968)
summary: Sinclair, author of The Jungle, argued for public ownership of industry, steep taxes on high incomes and inheritances, strong unions and a press free of wealth, and ran for governor of California in 1934 on the End Poverty in California (EPIC) plan of state production colonies and pensions.

public-ownership.rationale: Proposed that the people buy the nation's industrial plant with 5 percent bonds ('the plant we propose to buy is worth roughly one hundred billion dollars') and foresaw the nationalisation of the railroads first.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: His EPIC platform replaced the sales tax with a steeply graduated state income tax (30% on incomes of $50,000) and said he would 'put back the income tax at a figure which will take at least 30% of all incomes beyond $50,000'.

unions-good.rationale: Urged organising farmers and workers into nationwide bodies 'wielding the threat of the mass-strike', co-operative factories and labour banks, and denounced employers' blacklists and the 'open shop'.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Said he is 'a prohibitionist, to the dismay of my libertarian friends' because alcohol killed his father, and wrote in The Book of Life of putting 'in jail anyone who sells alcoholic drink'.

decide-locally.rationale: In his EPIC book he called it 'un-American' to trust affairs 'to the management of people three thousand miles away' and said even the Russians found they had to decentralise.

central-planning.rationale: Argued in Letters to Judd that with publicly owned plant 'we cut out the wastes and reduplication' and put five million unemployed to work, doubling production.

tax-inheritance.rationale: The EPIC platform called for a steeply graduated inheritance tax taking 50% of money above $50,000 bequeathed to an individual and 50% above $250,000; Letters to Judd urges putting the inheritance tax back and closing gift loopholes.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Told Judd that tariffs are taxes passed on to consumers and that 'carefully nourished infant industries grow up into highwaymen'.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Praised the founders' break with rule 'by grace of God' for 'a republic, owned and run by its citizens, all standing on an equal plane', foresaw 'a world-wide federation of republics', and ridiculed monarchs as 'degenerates' ruling 'by grace of God'.

military-superiority.rationale: In Letters to Judd he rejected the argument that armaments make the country safe, saying spending on them makes other nations do the same, 'so we might as well do our own destruction and have it over with'.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Wrote Mammonart as 'an interpretation of the arts from the point of view of the class struggle' and The Profits of Religion as 'an essay in economic interpretation' of the churches' role for the ruling classes.

production-for-use.rationale: His EPIC colonies were run for 'food production for use and not for profit', and his Letters to Judd argue that publicly owned industry would double production by cutting profit-driven waste.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Wrote that 'men are getting ready to try democracy in industry' and that industrial 'government of industry by the citizens of industry' is the step in progress, a higher type of society than 'industrial monarchy'.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Argued in The Book of Life that churches' divine commandments are in practice revised by 'human reason, and nothing but human reason', and that morality is 'a problem of continuous adjustment' rather than fixed ancient law.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Wrote in Letters to Judd: 'we believe that all men should be equal before the law... they all have equal rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness'.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: In his EPIC book he said that 'the action of our courts in vetoing acts of Congress and of State legislatures is wholly unconstitutional and arbitrary' and that it is 'intolerable that any small group of men should be permitted to balk the will of the people expressed at the polls'.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Wrote that divorce protects love and that 'except for grave offenses' no one should get one in under six months, after which a judge 'is required to grant the divorce' if the couple still wish it, on the Swiss model, without proof of fault.

cooperative-communities.rationale: His EPIC platform set up state land colonies with 'co-operative kitchens and cafeterias' and 'cultural centers' to 'explain the principles of co-operation' and he praised the Ruskin co-operative colony; they were state-run, not self-governing communities holding all property in common, so +1.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: The thesis of The Brass Check is that 'our newspapers do not represent public interests, but private interests; they do not represent humanity, but property'.

arms-reduction.rationale: Told Judd that government spends 'thirteen dollars to destroy' life for one to save it and that the military men's claim that armaments prevent attack is false because 'when we spend this money on armaments we cause other nations to do the same'.

women-suffrage.rationale: Recalled that he 'walked in the first suffrage parade in New York', behind Inez Milholland's white charger.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: The EPIC platform guaranteed 'every unemployed man and woman in the State' self-supporting work in state colonies, 'a living at the outset... comfort' later, and $50-a-month pensions for the old, blind and widows with children.

notes: Read by theme: Letters to Judd (1925), The Industrial Republic (1907), The Brass Check, The Profits of Religion, parts of The Goose-Step, and the 1933 EPIC book I, Governor of California. Twenty-three statements answered, almost all high or medium on taxes, public ownership, unions, tariffs and the press. Deeper pass: the Autobiography (66840), The Book of Life (38117) and Mammonart (69027) added no-fault-divorce, legalize-drugs (alcohol prohibitionist), women-suffrage, class-struggle-history and reason-over-faith. His 1917 decision to back the Allies (he later says he 'swallowed the British propaganda') is not used for the war statements: he had written a manifesto against war in 1914, then supported US entry, then regretted it, so no single position. Not answered: religion statements (The Profits of Religion argues the churches serve the rich, while in EPIC he says it is no campaign against any religion: no bank wording settled), land-value-tax (his 10% tax on idle land does not replace other taxes), and the Goose-Step on universities (academic freedom has no bank statement). Failing the uncertainty rule is the expected outcome unless noted otherwise.
